title: Test-time compute scaling
big_idea: You can buy accuracy at answer time instead of training time: let the model try many times, or revise its own work, and keep a good answer. The gain is only real if something can tell which try is right, and the best way to spend the compute depends on how hard the question is.

papers.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
papers.authors: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Ré, Mirhoseini
papers.what: Sampled the same model up to 10,000 times per problem on GSM8K, MATH, MiniF2F, CodeContests and SWE-bench Lite. Measured coverage (share of problems where any sample is right) and fit it with an exponentiated power law in the number of samples.
papers.result: Coverage grew with samples over four orders of magnitude. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 (single-sample state of the art was 43%). 5 DeepSeek tries solved 29.62% for $10.8 vs 24.00% for $39 with one GPT-4o try. On MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct, coverage went from 82.9% (100 samples) to 98.44% (10,000), but majority vote and reward models plateaued around 100 samples (best gain only 40.50% to 41.41%).
papers.takeaway: If your task has a cheap automatic checker (tests, a solver, a schema plus business rules), many cheap tries from a small local model can beat one expensive call. Without a checker, invest in verification before you invest in more samples.

papers.title: Archon: An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques
papers.authors: Saad-Falcon, Gamarra Lafuente, Natarajan, Maru, Todorov, Guha, Buchanan, Chen, Guha, Ré, Mirhoseini
papers.what: Treats inference-time techniques as modules (generator/ensemble, fuser, ranker, critic, verifier, unit-test generator and evaluator) stacked in layers, and uses Bayesian optimization to search a space of 9,576 configurations for the best stack under a compute budget.
papers.result: Searched stacks beat o1, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet by 15.1% on average across instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks; open-source-only stacks were 11.2% above prior open-source approaches. Bayesian optimization found the best stack in 96.0% of searches with 88.5% fewer evaluations than greedy search. Unit tests plus more samples raised CodeContests Pass@1 from 17.9% to 29.3%. The fuser helped on every benchmark (8.9% on average); verifiers helped most on reasoning tasks.
papers.takeaway: Don't hand-pick one trick. Build sampling, ranking, fusing and checking as swappable steps, then let a small eval set choose the stack per task.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
papers.what: On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, compared two ways to spend test-time compute: searching against a process reward model (best-of-N, beam search, lookahead) and a fine-tuned model that revises its own answer (sequential vs parallel). Questions were binned into 5 difficulty levels by the base model's own success rate over 2048 samples.
papers.result: The best method depends on difficulty: sequential revision did best on easy questions, a mix of sequential and parallel on harder ones; beam search beat best-of-N on medium-hard questions but over-optimized the verifier on easy ones. Choosing per difficulty matched or beat best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (abstract: more than 4x). FLOPs-matched, a small model with test-time compute beat a 14x larger model on questions where it had some success, but pretraining was better on the hardest questions or with high inference load.
papers.takeaway: Estimate difficulty first (for example, by how much a few samples agree), then route: easy questions get one try plus a revision, hard ones get more parallel tries, and the hardest may need a bigger model.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?
papers.authors: Schaeffer, Kazdan, Hughes, Juravsky, Price, Lynch, Jones, Kirk, Mirhoseini, Koyejo
papers.what: Explains why aggregate success with k attempts follows a power law even though each single problem's failure rate falls exponentially in k: the power law comes from a heavy left tail of very hard problems in the distribution of single-attempt success rates. Tested on Pythia models on MATH and frontier models on HarmBench jailbreaking.
papers.result: Proved the tail near zero (density like p^(b-1)) is necessary and sufficient for a k^(-b) power law. Cases without the heavy tail (e.g. Llama 3 8B IT, jailbroken on every prompt within budget) did not show a power law. A distributional estimator of the exponent had about an order of magnitude lower relative error than curve fitting, which the authors equate to roughly 2-4 orders of magnitude less inference compute.
papers.takeaway: Before buying a big sampling budget, sample a little, look at the per-problem success rates, and forecast. A task with many near-zero problems will be expensive to brute-force.

terms: Extra computation spent when answering (more samples, revisions, search) instead of when training.
Share of problems where at least one of k tries is right. An upper bound on what any picker can reach.
Asking the same question many times at a temperature above 0 so the tries differ.
Keep the answer that the most tries agree on. Needs no checker, but plateaus.
A model call that merges several candidates into one answer / that orders candidates and keeps the best.
Sequential: revise one answer step after step. Parallel: many independent tries, then pick.
Choosing how to spend test-time compute per question, based on its predicted difficulty.
traps: Reporting coverage (pass@k) as if it were accuracy. Coverage assumes you can always spot the right try; in production you usually can't.
Adding samples without a verifier. Brown et al. saw majority vote and reward models stall near 100 samples while coverage kept rising.
Sampling at temperature 0. Every try is the same, so more tries add nothing.
Counting calls instead of tokens. A fuser or revision call reads all candidates, so its cost grows with the number of candidates.
Assuming test-time compute always replaces a bigger model. Snell et al. found pretraining wins on the hardest questions and at high inference volume.
Choosing the strategy per difficulty on the same small set you then report on. That overfits; hold out data.
check: Coverage at k=100 is 90% but majority vote at k=100 is 45%. What is missing?
A good verifier. The model can produce the right answer, but the picker can't find it: that 45-point difference is the generation-verification gap.
Why can a per-problem failure rate fall exponentially while the average follows a power law?
Because the average mixes problems of different difficulty. A heavy tail of problems with near-zero single-try success makes the average fall slowly, like a power law (Schaeffer et al. 2025).
For an easy question, should you spend 4 calls on 4 parallel samples or on 1 sample plus 3 revisions?
Snell et al. found sequential revision best on easy questions, and a mix of both on harder ones. Test on your own task, since they used a fine-tuned revision model.
